title: Permissions
icon: ShieldCheck
description: How Applad decides who can read, create, update, and delete your data, enforced inside PostgreSQL with row-level security.

import { Database, Users, KeyRound } from 'lucide-react';

Every read and write in Applad passes a permission check. You describe who may do
what with short strings like `read("users")` or `delete("user:$id")`, and Applad
enforces them in the database itself using PostgreSQL row-level security. A rule
you set is a rule the database keeps, not one your client is trusted to honour.

This page explains the permission string format, the roles you can grant to, the
two layers where permissions live (the table and the row), and how enforcement
actually behaves. It applies anywhere data is accessed: the query builder, a
single row read, and schema-scoped SQL alike.

## Permission strings

A permission is a string of the form `action("role")`:

```text
read("users")
create("team:sales")
update("user:64b7f...")
delete("team:sales/owner")
```

The **action** is what the grant allows. The **role** in quotes is who it is
granted to.

### Actions

There are exactly four actions, one for each thing you can do to a row. Each maps
to one PostgreSQL command and the row-level security policy that guards it.

| Action | Allows | Enforced as |
|---|---|---|
| `read` | Reading the row: it appears in queries and single-row reads | `SELECT` policy (`USING`) |
| `create` | Inserting a new row into the table | `INSERT` policy (`WITH CHECK`) |
| `update` | Changing an existing row | `UPDATE` policy (`USING` and `WITH CHECK`) |
| `delete` | Removing a row | `DELETE` policy (`USING`) |
| `write` | Shorthand that expands to `update` **and** `delete` | (expanded, not stored) |

`write` is a convenience the SDKs accept. `write("user:$id")` is stored as
`update("user:$id")` and `delete("user:$id")`. There is no separate "write"
grant at rest, and no other actions exist. A permission with any other action is
rejected when you set it (`parsePermissionStrings` returns an error for any
action outside this set).

The pairing of `USING` and `WITH CHECK` on `update` matters: `USING` decides
which existing rows you may target, and `WITH CHECK` decides whether the row is
still permitted after your change. `create` has only `WITH CHECK` because there
is no prior row to test, which is also why `create` is table-level only (below).

## Roles

A role names an identity or a group. Applad recognises exactly these, and no
others:

| Role | Matches | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `any` | Everyone, including unauthenticated callers | `read("any")` |
| `users` | Any signed-in user | `create("users")` |
| `user:<id>` | One specific user, by their user ID | `update("user:64b7f...")` |
| `team:<id>` | Every member of a team | `read("team:sales")` |
| `team:<id>/<role>` | Only team members who hold a given role (for example `owner`, `admin`) | `delete("team:sales/owner")` |

There is no `guest`, `member`, or `label` role: an unauthenticated caller is
covered by `any`, and a signed-in one by `users`. The first two rows are
resolved from the presence of a user id alone; the last three are resolved from
the caller's identity and their [team](/build/teams) memberships (see below).

```dart
'read("any")'                 // public
'read("users")'               // any signed-in user
'update("user:$authorId")'    // just this user
'read("team:$channelId")'     // members of a team
'delete("team:$orgId/owner")' // team members with the "owner" role
```

Team roles come from [teams](/build/teams): when you add a member you may give them
roles, and each `team:<id>/<role>` grant matches members holding that role.

<Callout title="Roles are resolved on the server, never sent by the client">
The caller never states their own roles. On every request Applad derives them
from the authenticated identity: `any` for everyone, plus `users` and
`user:<id>` once signed in, plus one `team:<id>` for each team the user belongs
to and one `team:<id>/<role>` for each role they hold in it. A client cannot add
`team:sales` to its request to read a team's data. This is why the permission
model is safe to expose to end-user code.
</Callout>

## Two layers: table and document

Permissions live in two places, and access is granted when **either** grants it.

### Table-level permissions

Set on the table, these apply to every row in it. Pass them when you create the
table (see [databases](/build/databases)):

```dart
final db = client.databases;

await db.createTable(
  databaseId: 'app',
  tableId: 'posts',
  name: 'posts',
  permissions: [
    'read("any")',      // anyone may read any post
    'create("users")',  // any signed-in user may add one
  ],
);
```

Here every post is world-readable and any signed-in user can create one.
`update` and `delete` are granted to nobody, so no one can edit or remove a post
through the API.

### Document (per-row) security

Turn on `documentSecurity` and each row can also carry its own permissions. A
row is then reachable if the table grants access **or** the row grants it:

```dart
await db.createTable(
  databaseId: 'app',
  tableId: 'messages',
  name: 'messages',
  permissions: ['create("users")'], // who may insert; no table-wide read
  documentSecurity: true,           // each row also carries its own permissions
);

await db.createRow(
  databaseId: 'app',
  tableId: 'messages',
  data: {'body': 'hello'},
  permissions: [
    'read("team:$channelId")',   // the channel's team can read
    'update("user:$authorId")',  // only the author can edit
    'delete("user:$authorId")',  // only the author can delete
  ],
);
```

With no table-level `read` grant, a message is visible only to those its own
`read(...)` permissions name. Per-row permissions cover `read`, `update`, and
`delete`. **`create` is table-level only**: a row cannot pre-authorise its own
insertion, so a `create(...)` entry in a row's permissions is ignored. To insert
a row, the table's `create` grant must admit the caller.

`updateRow` and `createRow` both take a `permissions` list, so you can change a
row's own permissions the same way you change its data.

<Callout title="The two layers are a union, never an override">
A row is reachable if the table grants access **or** the row grants it. A
per-row permission cannot take away access the table already gives, and a table
grant cannot be narrowed by a row. If you need a row visible only to its author,
do not grant table-level `read` at all and let the row's own `read(...)` decide.
Internally the two clauses are combined with `OR`, so adding a grant in either
place only ever widens who gets in.
</Callout>

## Enforcement

Permissions are compiled into PostgreSQL row-level security policies on the
underlying table. Applad runs each request under a restricted database role with
the caller's identity and resolved roles set on the session, so the policies
decide every query, not the API code around them.

Two consequences worth relying on:

- **It holds everywhere.** The fluent query builder, a direct row read, and
  schema-scoped SQL run under the same policies. There is no privileged read
  path that skips them.
- **It fails closed and stays quiet.** A row you lack `read` on is not an error,
  it is simply absent from your results. A query returns the rows you may see and
  no indication that others exist. An update or delete you are not granted
  affects nothing.

### Where document security changes the check

Turning `documentSecurity` on is what enables row-level security on the
underlying PostgreSQL table. With it on, the policies described here run inside
the database for every statement, and the silent-filtering behaviour above
applies. With it off, the table has no per-row policies: its table-level grants
are checked in the API before the write or single-row read runs, and a caller
the table does not admit is refused. Either way the grant is enforced before any
data comes back; document security decides whether the enforcement lives in the
database or in front of it.

## The SQL mechanism

If you want to know exactly what "enforced in the database" means, here is the
shape of it. Two stores back a table:

- The **table-level grants** live in a `permissions` metadata row per
  `(table, action, role)`. These drive the table half of each policy.
- A **document-security table** also gains a hidden `_permissions` JSONB column,
  shaped `{"read":[...],"update":[...],"delete":[...]}`, holding each row's own
  grants. `create` never appears here: a row cannot pre-authorise its own
  insertion.

On every request Applad opens a transaction, sets the caller's identity into
PostgreSQL session settings, and switches to a restricted per-database role
(`..._authenticated` for a signed-in caller, `..._anon` otherwise) with
`SET LOCAL ROLE` so the policies actually bind. The caller's resolved roles are
written into `request.jwt.claims`, and their user id into `applad.user_id`.

Each role in a grant compiles to a boolean test against those settings:

| Role | Compiles to (roughly) |
|---|---|
| `any` | `TRUE` |
| `users` | `applad.user_id` is set |
| `user:<id>` | `applad.user_id` equals that id |
| `team:<id>` and `team:<id>/<role>` | `jsonb_exists(claims -> 'roles', 'team:<id>')` |

Team roles are tested with `jsonb_exists` rather than the PostgreSQL `?`
operator on purpose: the query layer rewrites a literal `?` into a bind
placeholder, which would corrupt the policy SQL. For a document-security table
each action's policy is the table clause `OR`-ed with a per-row clause that
scans the row's `_permissions` array for the action and checks each listed role
the same way. A separate **restrictive** policy pins every row to its owning
project, so no policy a project writes can ever reach another project's data.

<Callout type="warn" title="Group permissions need the role resolver">
`team:<id>` grants only match when Applad can resolve a caller's memberships
server-side. That resolver is wired in by default. If it were absent, a
`team:<id>` grant would match no one rather than everyone: the safe direction to
fail. A caller can never assert a `team:` role itself.
</Callout>

## Sessions, API keys, and the console

The same permission model runs for every caller. What differs is only which
roles a caller resolves to.

- **A client session** (a user's JWT) resolves to `any`, `users`,
  `user:<their id>`, and one `team:<id>` plus `team:<id>/<role>` for every team
  they have joined. This is the full model, and it is what per-row permissions
  are designed for.
- **A server API key** authenticates as the project rather than as a person. It
  resolves to `any` and `users` but to no `user:<id>` and no team roles, since a
  key has no memberships. A key therefore reads and writes through table-level
  grants for `any` and `users`, but it is not a permission bypass: rows fenced to
  a specific user or team by their own permissions are not visible to a key. A
  key's reach is additionally narrowed by its **scopes**, which decide the
  routes it may call at all before the permission model is even consulted.
- **The console** acts as an administrator over a project's structure. Defining
  tables, columns, and table-level grants is done here (or from a key or a
  migration), which is why setup is described as an API-key task below.

<Callout title="Why a key is not a superuser">
Some backends let a server key ignore permissions entirely. Applad does not: a
key runs under the same row-level security as everyone else, with the roles of
an anonymous-plus-signed-in principal and nothing more. To have a key operate on
per-user rows, grant the table `create("users")` and set an owner column, or
write the row's permissions explicitly. There is no request field that lets any
caller name its own roles; doing so would let anyone mint `team:admin` and pass
every check.
</Callout>

## A worked example: a chat app

Messages readable by everyone in a channel but editable only by their author:

```dart
// Once, at setup (from an API key, migration, or the console):
await db.createTable(
  databaseId: 'chat',
  tableId: 'messages',
  name: 'messages',
  permissions: ['create("users")'], // any signed-in user may post
  documentSecurity: true,
);

// Each time a user sends a message:
await db.createRow(
  databaseId: 'chat',
  tableId: 'messages',
  data: {'channel_id': channelId, 'body': body},
  permissions: [
    'read("team:$channelId")',   // the channel team reads it
    'update("user:$authorId")',  // the author edits it
    'delete("user:$authorId")',  // the author deletes it
  ],
);
```

Now a member of the channel's team sees the message when they list the channel,
a non-member's query never returns it, and only the author's session can edit or
remove it. No check runs in your app code, and none can be bypassed by a crafted
request.

## Owner columns

If a `documentSecurity` table has a column named `owner_id` (or `user_id`),
Applad adds an owner policy: the signed-in user whose ID matches that column has
full access to the row, in addition to any table or row grants. This lets a
"belongs to me" table work from the column alone, without writing a
`user:<id>` permission onto every row.

```dart
await db.createTable(
  databaseId: 'app',
  tableId: 'notes',
  name: 'notes',
  permissions: ['create("users")'],
  documentSecurity: true,
);
await db.createStringColumn(
  databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'notes', key: 'owner_id', required_: true,
);
// A row where owner_id equals the caller's user ID is fully theirs.
```

Set `owner_id` to the creating user's ID and that user can read, update, and
delete their own notes with no per-row permissions at all. `owner_id` is
preferred over `user_id` if both are present.

## Setting permissions from the console or an API key

Defining tables, columns, and their table-level permissions is a setup task. Do
it once from the console, a migration, or a server script authenticated with an
API key, not from end-user code. Per-row permissions, by contrast, are set on
each write and are safe to build from client code, because the roles a caller
can grant to are still resolved from that caller's own identity.
